title: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Brine-shrimp abdomen grows relatively longer the saltier the water

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: In brine-shrimps (Artemia), increasing salinity changes the relative rates of growth of body parts, the abdomen growing relatively longer compared with the cephalothorax the salter the water, so that forms described as distinct species correspond to ranges of water density.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: _Pari passu_ with these changes, there is a marked change in the relative lengths of the fore and hind portions of the body, that is to say, of the “cephalothorax” and abdomen: the latter growing relatively longer, the salter the water.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Osmotic factors in growth”. Scope: brine-shrimps (Artemia) in waters of varying salinity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-26: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predictor, response ratio, and direction are explicit and experimentally discriminating. Public data likely cover some strains and salinities, but a broad species-level test would require harmonizing multiple studies.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure abdomen-to-cephalothorax length in Artemia raised or sampled across salinity gradients and fit the ratio as a function of salinity while controlling species, sex, age, and population. A consistently positive salinity effect supports the claim; no effect or a negative effect refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Morphometric data paired with exact salinity are scattered.

Genetic differentiation and age can confound environmental plasticity.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The ratio and the salinity axis are directly measurable, and several experimental and field studies already report both. There is no single downloadable morphometric database, so a test means compiling those tables, which cover multiple populations but not a balanced global design. Population identity and co-varying water chemistry remain serious alternative explanations of the same body proportions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress the abdomen-to-cephalothorax length ratio of Artemia on salinity, holding temperature and food as covariates and comparing populations raised across a salinity series. A positive slope, with named 'species' falling on successive parts of one curve, would support the claim; a flat or negative slope after those controls would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wild samples confound salinity with temperature, food and clonal lineage.

Thompson's own isotonic-versus-equal-density test is still not a standard column in those tables.

Morphometrics sit in paper tables rather than one open archive.
